text.p: The Victorian state government forecast on Wednesday a 1996/97 underlying budget deficit of A$700,000, well below the estimated deficit of A$14.0 million it unveiled four months ago and said it was on track for a credit rating upgrade.
Announcing the state's budget for the year to June 30, Treasurer Alan Stockdale said the underlying outcome for 1995/96 was a surplus of A$474 million against an estimated deficit of A$344 million.
Counting the A$4.7 billion windfall from the proceeds of the Victoria government's sell-off of electricity assets, the headline surplus for 1995/96 was A$5.1 billion.

The headline surplus for 1996/97 is estimated at A$2.17 billion, including net capital proceeds of A$1.5 billion from the sale of the 1,600 megawatt Hazelwood coal-fired power station in August, the budget papers show.

The improvement in the estimated underlying budget position for 1996/97 comes despite a A$100 million addition to the size of national-government grants assumed for 1996/97 in Victoria government's May economic statement.
"The (1996/97) budget involves additional allocations of close to A$300 million to improve education, health and other services to Victoria's people," Stockdale told parliament.
The sale of Hazelwood was the most recent of a string of privatisations in the energy sector, which will have cut net public sector debt to A$19 billion by the end of 1996/97, Stockdale said.
"We are on track to maintaining the zero budget deficit target," Stockdale told reporters an hour before before giving his budget speech to state parliament.
"We are now on course to return to a AAA credit rating before the turn of the century," he told parliament later.
Victoria state debt is currently rated at AA by Standard & Poor's Corp and Aa2 by Moody's Investors Service.

"It accommodates reductions in Commonwealth grants exceeding A$200 million this year without increasing taxes as other states have done. Despite these costs, the government today delivers a virtually balanced budget."
The budget, which makes no major new announcements since the May economic statement, assumes state economic growth of three percent and headline inflation of two percent in 1996/97.
The growth rate is unchanged from the forecast in May, but the inflation rate is lower than the previous estimate of 3.25 percent, due partly to the July cut on official interest rates.
